title: Regiment and Typewriter
premise: In 1917, Mara Whitlock drives for her mother, the suffragist Edith Whitlock, and secretly reads every letter she delivers, keeping a ledger of the town's secrets and names. When the army requisitions the coastal town of Harrow Point as a staging ground, the ledger — with every name in it — becomes evidence the military wants destroyed, and the Whitlock family is pulled into a web of surveillance, loyalty, and betrayal. As evacuation orders come and a troop ship prepares to sail on the morning tide, Mara must decide who among her fractured family takes the last berth: her mother, whose cause has cost them everything; her brother, a deserter hiding in the lighthouse; or herself. In the end, Mara gives up her place, burns the ledger page by page to protect the town's names, and stays behind — discovering that belonging is not a berth on a ship but the choice to remain answerable to the people you love.
about_author: Coral Galloway is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing wartime correspondence in coastal county records. She writes historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Weight of Paper
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She drives her mother Edith between suffrage meetings along the coast, reading letters in the motorcar and recording names in her private ledger. Establishes her belief that information is power and that she is its honest keeper. Emotional beat: quiet pride curdling into unease when a letter mentions 'requisition' and 'Harrow Point.'

chapters.title: Khaki at the Gate
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Soldiers arrive overnight; the town green becomes a supply depot and the harbor is closed. Edith protests publicly while Mara notices an officer, Captain Renshaw, watching their house. Emotional beat: the family's sense of home dissolving as barbed wire goes up around the churchyard.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Knows
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Renshaw visits, politely demanding all correspondence held by 'agitators.' Mara realizes her ledger — every name, every secret, including her brother Tom's desertion — is exactly what they want. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into resolve; she hides the ledger inside the spare tire well.

chapters.title: Tom in the Lighthouse
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, Tom. Hiding in the decommissioned lighthouse, Tom watches troop ships and wrestles with shame. Mara brings him food and news; he begs her to burn his pages from the ledger. Emotional beat: sibling tenderness strained by the question of what protection actually costs.

chapters.title: Edith's Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Arrested after a rally, Edith spends a night in the requisitioned schoolhouse and sees how the officers run the town like a machine. She returns hardened, willing to use Mara's ledger as leverage. Emotional beat: Mara's horror that her mother would trade other people's secrets for the cause.

chapters.title: The Requisition Order
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Evacuation is announced: one civilian ship, limited berths, departure on the morning tide. The army searches houses for documents; Renshaw gives Mara three days to surrender the ledger in exchange for guaranteed passage. Emotional beat: the theme crystallizes — everything must now be measured by what can be carried.

chapters.title: Names We Owe
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Neighbors beg Mara for help using what she knows; she can save some families with her information but exposing it endangers everyone in the book. A betrayal — a neighbor reports Tom's hiding place to win a berth. Emotional beat: guilt and the corruption of small powers wielded desperately.

chapters.title: Three Berths, Four Souls
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. The family confronts the arithmetic: Edith, Tom, Mara, and young cousin Nell — one berth short. Edith argues the movement needs her; Tom argues a deserter deserves nothing. Emotional beat: love turning cruel under pressure; Nell silently packs her one allowed bag.

chapters.title: The Burning Ledger
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, climax. Rather than surrender it, Mara burns the ledger page by page on the beach before Renshaw's soldiers, freeing the town's names from both army and cause alike. Tom surrenders himself to buy Edith and Nell their berths. Emotional beat: cathartic destruction; identity severed from record.

chapters.title: Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, resolution. She puts Edith and Nell aboard and stays behind with Tom awaiting transport to court-martial, choosing to remain as witness and advocate. Renshaw, unsettled by her defiance, lets her visit the prisoners. Emotional beat: hard-won belonging — Mara belongs not to a ship or a movement but to the people left standing beside her.
